blocks.cap: A second hand in the seams, working the opposite way

blocks.p: Rei followed the second aftertaste from the widow's door across three wards. It taught him something the Healer's threads never could. There was another worker in this city. Gin's mercy closed wounds and bound the grateful into one careful tally. This other thing tore.

blocks.break: The underpass by the freight line

blocks.p: The trail ended at the long pedestrian underpass beneath the station, where the freight line crossed overhead. The low end flooded whenever it rained, and the tiles there were stained to the height of a child. Rei knew this place from Gin's pages. He had read them so often that he could recite them.

doc.title: Gin's archive. Disturbed Areas. The Station Underpass
lines: Walked the freight underpass again. Still wrong on the 11th. Did not stay. G.U.
THIN SPOT. A migrating thin spot. Worst in the cold.
A place where the membrane has worn through... and the wear migrates with the district's mood.
A Grid handler keeps a dog at the south mouth most nights. The CVD flags it. The Grid actually watches it.
Everything is more visible to everyone here... and entities see you regardless of rank. Carry less stability in than you think you need.
I have crossed easiest, and been noticed worst, in that underpass. The two turn out to be the same fact wearing different coats.

blocks.p: The dog was there at the south mouth, a heavy brown animal lying on a folded blanket with its chin on its paws. It lifted its head when Rei came down the steps and watched him without moving. It did not follow him in. Rei took that as the warning it was.

It was August, not winter, and the underpass should have been at its quietest. It was not quiet. The membrane here was not being soothed. It was being abraded, scored thin on purpose, the way a lock is sanded until the bolt gives. Where Gin's seams felt like a tourniquet, these felt like a held breath before a window breaks. Rei's gift recoiled so hard that he tasted copper.

Under the scoring there was something older, and he recognised it from Gin's book too. It was heavy and it was not thinking. The 2011 dead had never been properly seen home, and their grief had gathered in the low places of the city like rainwater. Gin had written about exactly this.

doc.title: CVD Entity Classification Reference. Chapter 11. Suffering Beings
lines: A suffering being is not an entity in the conventional sense. It is the residue of an intelligence... the emotional material that remained after the self dissolved at crossing, concentrated in the location where the dissolution occurred.
It is not thinking. It is not choosing. It is not directing its effects at anyone. It simply weighs what it weighs, and if you are in the space, you feel the weight.
The person is gone. Demons retain intelligence. Spirits retain personality. Suffering beings have no continuity with the person they came from.

It cannot be reasoned with, communicated with, redirected, or resolved through relationship. It can only be cleared, or managed. This is not exorcism. There is nothing to remove. There is something to process.

Margin, G.U. A suffering being is grief that found no floor to land on. After 2011 there was a great deal of grief and nowhere near enough floor. Be gentle when you meet one. It was a person's love before it was your problem.

blocks.p: That was what the boy in Gin's ledger had been hearing in the gutters when it rained. Not voices. Weight. And someone was using that weight now like sandpaper against the wall.

blocks.break: A back room the Grid kept that month

blocks.p: The Grid had a name for the one doing it. Rei got it in a back room above a shuttered shop, a room the Grid happened to be using that month and would not be using the next. He was there on a vouch. One of Gin's nodes, one of the people who owed his brother the dangerous kind of debt, had vouched for him to a man, and the man had sent him here. Nobody in the room was in charge. People came up the stairs, put something down or picked something up, and left. A courier sat on an upturned crate with a kit bag on her knees that had come, she said, through three pairs of hands before hers, and would go through one more before it reached the person who needed it.
She gave Rei the name over her shoulder, while she checked the bag's straps, in the particular hush people use for things they hope are exaggerations.

"They call it the Inverted God," she said. "Or its aspirant does. It isn't a god yet. Its mouth is a boy called Kaito. He was a medium before he was a vessel, and now there's not much left of him but the mouth." She pulled a strap tight. "The thing itself doesn't come to the pools. It sits somewhere else, in somebody else, and talks through him."
"What does it want?"

"It says the veil is a muzzle the living strapped onto the dead. It says tearing it isn't a catastrophe, it's emancipation." She looked at him properly then. "The old people say there's something at the centre that holds the wall shut. This one wants to be the opposite of that. It wants to tear the wall open and rule whatever pours through. It doesn't want a seat at the table. It wants to turn the table over and salt the ground where it stood."
By every measure the factions could take, she said, it was the larger horror in this city by an order of magnitude. Then she shouldered the bag and went down the stairs, and someone else came up.

That was exactly the problem, and Rei felt the shape of it close around him in that back room like a hand. The moment there was a bigger monster, every faction with a grade and a grievance would turn toward it. And the quiet, reasonable, mercy-minting thing wearing his brother would become, by sheer comparison, the lesser evil. The manageable one. The one a sensible person might even ally with against the worse. The Healer had not summoned the Inverted God. But in its long patient existence it had never been handed a better gift than a rival monstrous enough to make it look like salvation.

blocks.cap: The sermon, and the true things stacked wrong

blocks.p: Kaito preached in a drained municipal pool in the dead hour after midnight. The pool had been closed since the summer before, and the blue paint on its walls had cracked into maps of countries that did not exist. About forty people stood on the tiled floor of the deep end. They all had the look of the widow. Accounted for. Grateful. Leashed. Except their leashes ran the other way, toward tearing instead of binding.

Kaito was younger than the dread around him had suggested. He could not have been more than twenty. He stood in the shallow end with his hands loose at his sides, and his eyes did not quite track the people he looked at, as if someone else were doing the looking through them. He did not rant. He grieved, out loud, with a precision that made the cicadas outside sound like applause.

"They drowned in front of us," he said of 2011. "And we built a wall so we would not have to keep hearing them, and we called the wall mercy." He let the words go out over the empty water lines. "Since 2009 the wall here in Kita has been failing. Since 2011 it has been failing faster. They tell you that is the danger. I tell you it is the dead, knocking. I am only proposing we stop lying about what the wall is."
Forty heads nodded. Rei's own head, traitorously, wanted to.

And there it was again, the angle, the murderous tilt under the true thing. Kaito was right that the membrane was partly a wall the living had built to stop hearing the dead. He was wrong, catastrophically and terminally wrong, about what happens to a city when the wall comes down. Rei stood at the lip of the empty pool with the ghost of chlorine in his nose. He understood that he was now holding two arguments, and each of them held enough truth to drown a person. His brother's captor was the more patient of the two, and the more polite. And politeness was going to be mistaken for safety by everyone with the power to act.
Kaito found him on the way out. These things always seemed to. He fell into step beside Rei on the cracked path to the gate, and he knew Rei's name, which meant the seams had been talking.

"Your brother and I want opposite things," he said, almost kindly. His voice was a young man's voice, but the words had an older weight in them, as if they had been chosen somewhere far away and only delivered here. "That should comfort you. It won't. You've already worked out that opposite things can want the same Tuesday."
He let that sit. Then he stopped at the gate and said, "When the seat comes vacant, ask yourself who benefits from the wall being thin. It isn't only me."

Rei walked home through the lantern-lit streets with that sentence in his chest. At the flat he did not sleep. He took Gin's archive down again and turned to the chapter on the Grid. He had been inside it for a week on a stranger's vouch, and he did not understand what he had walked into. Gin would have written it down.
